fields.title: Parus: The Metric Went Up, But Something Is Off
fields.summary: The quarter's key number is the best all year. Decide what you will investigate.
fields.decisionPrompt: How will you investigate the situation and what will you propose at planning?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager for Parus.
fields.brief/company: Parus is a fictional family budget planning app: 620 thousand monthly active users, 8% paid subscribers.
fields.brief/context: The quarter's key metric—users logging at least one transaction per week—grew by 23%, the best result of the year. The team is commended. At the same time, support reports a flood of angry emails, and subscription revenue hasn't changed.
fields.brief/objective: Understand what actually happened and decide what to do.
fields.brief/constraints: One analyst, one researcher, three weeks until next quarter's planning.
fields.brief/task: Choose how you will investigate and justify your choice.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: When a Metric Becomes a Target, It Ceases to Be a Good Measure
fields.learnTakeaway/body: As soon as a bonus is tied to a number, someone finds a way to bump it without delivering real value. The fix isn't finding a flawless metric, but building a system: driver metrics reveal what drove the growth, while guardrail metrics show the price paid. Match your method to the decision deadline: a two-day breakdown that changes a choice is better than a quarterly study that arrives too late.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
Users logging a transaction per week: 214k → 263k over the quarter (+23%).

Quarterly changes: at the start, released a reminder 'log your daily expenses'—a daily push notification at 21:00 to all users.

Average transactions per user: was 11 per week, became 7.

Share of users opening monthly summary: was 38%, became 24%.

Subscription rate: 8.1% → 8.0%. Revenue unchanged.

Churn of users onboarded over half a year ago: was 3.1% per month, became 4.4%.

17% of audience disabled notifications completely (was 6%).
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Support tickets per 100 active users: was 1.2, became 2.9.

Frequent topics: 'how to disable these notifications'—41% of new tickets; 'the app became pushy'—18%; 'I logged a transaction and it's in the wrong category'—22%.

The last issue appeared because the reminder features a quick amount input, while the category is auto-assigned—guessing right about half the time.

App store rating for the quarter: 4.6 → 4.1. Reviews frequently mention 'feels like nagging'.

Support brought this up twice in meetings. Both times the conversation pivoted back to key metric growth.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
The primary metric was assigned a year ago: users logging at least one transaction per week. At the time, it accurately reflected value: budget keepers renew subscriptions 2.6 times more often.

No guardrail metrics were defined: churn and support tickets are checked quarterly on request.

No driver metrics exist either; usage depth (transactions, opening monthly summary) isn't shown on the main dashboard.

The team's quarterly OKR was set to '+20% to the primary metric', with bonuses tied directly to it.

Last year a similar case occurred in another team: 'app opens' was bumped with a popup, then rolled back.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
The CPO is pleased and suggests doubling down: add a second reminder in the morning.

Marketing requests a study on 'why people stop budgeting'—a large, qualitative quarterly project.

The analyst says they can run breakdowns in two days if told which ones to look at.

The researcher is available starting next week.

Next quarter planning is in three weeks; that's when a decision to double down on reminders or roll them back will be made.

Technically, rolling back notifications takes one day.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Set up guardrail metrics and break down growth
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Break down growth by cohorts and depth in two days, surface churn and support tickets as guardrails, and scope qualitative research down to focused chats about categories.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
The two-day breakdowns reveal the full picture: growth came from users logging exactly one transaction per week—prompted by the push—while average transactions dropped from 11 to 7 and monthly summary views fell from 38% to 24%.
Guardrail metrics are added to the main dashboard: veteran churn 3.1% → 4.4%, support tickets 1.2 → 2.9, notifications disabled 6% → 17%.
It becomes clear the metric no longer measures its original intent: it tracks response to push notifications, not budgeting.
The researcher spends a week conducting eight interviews—not on general budgeting habits, but on specific actions following notifications and issues with category misclassifications.
At planning, you propose rolling back daily pushes, keeping them opt-in, and switching the primary metric to engagement depth.
Trade-off: the team loses its headline result and bonus tied to the metric—it was a tough conversation.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: The metric grew by 23%, the best result all year. Add a second morning reminder and solidify success.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
The morning reminder adds another 9% to the primary metric—formally repeating the win.
Disabled notifications reach 26%, support tickets hit 3.8 per 100 active users, and app store rating drops to 3.9.
Veteran user churn hits 5.1% per month; over six months this significantly exceeds all new acquisition growth.
Subscription revenue remains flat.
Two quarters later, reminders must be rolled back completely, and the metric falls below its original baseline.
Trade-off: the harm signal was present from day one—support raised it twice—but without guardrail metrics, there was nothing driving action.
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Marketing is right: we need to understand why people stop budgeting altogether. A quarter of qualitative research will provide depth.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
The study launches and runs its full three months.
Meanwhile, the decision on reminders is made without it at planning three weeks later—and made in favor of doubling down, as no counterarguments were brought to the table.
The final report is insightful yet broad: people quit budgeting when they don't see results. While true, it doesn't answer the quarter's core decision.
The data breakdowns the analyst could have produced in two days were never requested.
Trade-off: you chose the longest method for a decision due in three weeks, rendering the research irrelevant to the outcome.
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: The metric proved flawed: it can be gaming with notifications. Set usage depth as primary and base next quarter's goal on it.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The conclusion is valid and critical: a target metric tied to bonuses stopped reflecting actual value.
The new primary metric—average transactions and summary views—is far harder to game.
However, changing the metric doesn't resolve what to do with reminders: at planning they are kept because no concrete action plan was proposed.
Guardrail metrics remain unmonitored, leaving future gaming attempts just as invisible.
Over the quarter, usage depth partially recovers, but churn remains elevated.
Trade-off: half of the right conclusion was made—you changed the metric while leaving the root cause active.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Research isn't tied to a decision or concrete choices
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Metrics form a flat list without primary, driver, and guardrail roles
